The initial wet body mass of newly released juvenile Hediste diversicolor is remarkably small, with offspring emerging from the egg capsule at approximately 4.2 × 10⁻⁶ grams [Ww0 = approximately 4.2 × 10⁻⁶ grams], a weight derived from the average egg diameter of roughly 200 micrometres. Field observations indicate that larvae undergo a critical larval metamorphosis once they have developed nineteen setigers, at which point the average length at metamorphosis reaches 0.36 cm . This morphological transformation marks the transition from a pelagic trochophore larva to a benthic juvenile worm capable of burrowing into the sediment. These early life-history stages are heavily influenced by ambient temperature, and laboratory studies conducted at a constant 18 °C [T = 18 °C] reveal that the onset of external feeding, marking the age at birth, occurs approximately 6.3 days [ab = approximately 6.3 days] after fertilisation. The feeding larvae then progress through a period of exogenous feeding until metamorphosis, which under the same thermal regime of 18 °C [T = 18 °C] occurs around 34.3 days  after fertilisation.

Under a contrasting temperature regime more typical of winter conditions in northern European estuaries, the developmental schedule shifts substantially. At a mean in situ temperature of 8.5 °C [T = 8.5 °C], the period required for metamorphosis lengthens dramatically to approximately 70 days . This deceleration of ontogeny reflects the strong temperature dependence of polychaete larval physiology and is consistent with patterns observed in other nereidid species. Once metamorphosis is complete, the recently metamorphosed juvenile begins a growth phase that depends critically on food availability and local hydrographic conditions. At an intermediate temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], individuals reach a wet weight at age 60 days of approximately 0.030 grams , indicating a period of rapid mass accumulation during the early juvenile stage. This weight gain is supported by the species' capacity for high ingestion rates; measurements in the laboratory at 15 °C [T = 15 °C] demonstrate a maximum ingestion rate of 132 joules per day , a feeding capacity that enables the sustained growth observed under optimal conditions.

Progressing through the sub-adult phase, individuals continue to gain both length and mass until they approach the critical transition to reproductive maturity. The wet weight at puberty, marking the onset of gametogenesis, has been recorded at 0.08 grams [Wwp = 0.08 grams], a size that typically corresponds to the attainment of a specific body length. Measurements of body length at this stage indicate that the maximum length at first reproduction reaches 14.7 cm [Li = 14.7 cm], although the size of the third setiger-bearing segment, L3, at the time of first reproduction attains a maximum of only 0.47 cm , highlighting the allometric growth patterns characteristic of this species. The transition to first reproduction in terms of age is documented under controlled salinity conditions of 19 psu. At a temperature of 16.3 °C [T = 16.3 °C], the estimated time to first reproduction is approximately 67 days after hatching [tR = approximately 67 days after hatching]. This relatively rapid onset of reproductive capability is an adaptation to the unpredictable and often ephemeral nature of the intertidal habitats the species occupies.

Once reproductively active, the species exhibits a life-history strategy in which first reproduction and death are closely linked, a pattern typical of semelparous nereidids that undergo epitokous metamorphosis. At a temperature of 17.4 °C [T = 17.4 °C] and a salinity of 19 psu, the age at first reproduction, which corresponds to the age at death for this semelparous species, has been estimated at 112 days [am = 112 days]. At the time of death, individuals show considerable variation in body mass depending on environmental context, but terminal wet weight at death has been recorded at 1.57 grams [Wwi = 1.57 grams]. The corresponding dry weight at death is considerably lower, measured at 0.27 grams , reflecting the high water content of the body tissues typical of soft-bodied polychaetes. These terminal measurements represent the culmination of a growth trajectory that begins with the minute larval mass and proceeds through the rapid juvenile and sub-adult phases, with the reproductive event itself consuming a substantial portion of the somatic reserves accumulated over the organism's lifetime. The trade-off between somatic growth and reproductive investment is stark in this species.

Interpopulation variation in life-history traits across the species' geographic range is substantial, reflecting local adaptation to different thermal and salinity regimes. In southern European populations, the warmer temperatures accelerate development such that the onset of external feeding can be as brief as approximately 6.3 days [ab = approximately 6.3 days] at 18 °C, while the larval metamorphosis is similarly compressed to about 34.3 days  at 18 °C. at a at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]In contrast, boreal populations experiencing mean in situ temperatures near 8.5 °C produce a metamorphosis schedule lasting approximately 70 days , a duration that is over twice as long as that observed in warmer-water conspecifics at a temperature of 8.5 °C [T = 8.5 °C]. This thermal plasticity has profound consequences for recruitment dynamics and population persistence. The species' broad salinity tolerance, from nearly freshwater conditions up to fully marine salinities of 35 psu, further contributes to its success as a dominant infaunal component of estuarine soft sediments. Its ability to sustain a maximum ingestion rate of 132 joules per day  at 15 °C allows it to exploit a wide range of organic detritus and microphytobenthos, fuelling the rapid growth needed to achieve the 14.7 cm body length at first reproduction within a single growing season in many habitats at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C].
